pr.title: Prepare Rust 1.80.1 point release
pr.description:
The point release is scheduled to include:

* https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/128271
* https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/128618
pr.author: emilyalbini

analysis.summary: Rust 1.80.1 includes a confirmed JumpThreading miscompilation fix: the pass reduced floating-point Eq/Ne comparisons to integer/bit-pattern comparisons of ScalarInts. Because float equality does not follow bit patterns (-0.0 == 0.0 although their bits differ; NaN != NaN), it could prove the wrong condition and thread control flow to the wrong branch. The fix makes process_assign bail out for floating-point constants. The same point release also reverts unrelated dead_code lint changes, but the reusable pass-level knowledge is the JumpThreading float-comparison bug.
analysis.originalLogic: JumpThreading's process_assign resolves a boolean assignment from an Eq/Ne comparison by taking the compared constant, normalizing it, converting it to a ScalarInt with `try_to_scalar_int()?`, and matching that integer value against tracked `Condition` values. For Eq it uses `ScalarInt::TRUE` and for Ne `ScalarInt::FALSE`; other BinOps return None. This was intended to thread conditions when the compared operand's constant was known.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: When the compared constant had a floating-point type, the historical pass still converted it to a ScalarInt and used integer/bit-pattern comparison against tracked conditions as though that established float equality. That is invalid: -0.0 and +0.0 have different bit patterns but compare equal, while NaN compares unequal to everything including itself. The pass could therefore fold/thread a float `==` or `!=` condition to the wrong successor block, producing a miscompilation. The corrected transform returns None for floating-point constants instead of comparing their bit patterns.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR in which a floating-point-typed value has a compile-time-known constant (for example propagated from a constant-selected branch) and is then compared with `==` or `!=` against a floating-point constant. Relevant values include -0.0, +0.0, NaN, infinities, and ordinary floats; the bug class is any float whose IEEE equality behavior differs from its bit pattern.
analysis.trigger: A float comparison of the form `if x == C` or `if x != C` where JumpThreading knows x's constant and processes the resulting boolean assignment. Minimal example from the regression test: `let x = if true { -0.0 } else { 1.0 }; if x == 0.0 { 0 } else { 1 }`.
preconditions: The operation is a comparison represented as Eq or Ne (the only BinOps mapped to ScalarInt::TRUE/FALSE in this code path).
The compared operand is a constant that JumpThreading can normalize and convert with try_to_scalar_int.
The compared constant's type is floating point, so bit-pattern equality is not equivalent to language equality.
A tracked condition on that value makes the pass attempt to prove which branch is taken.
pitfalls: -0.0 == 0.0 is true even though their ScalarInt bit patterns differ.
NaN != NaN is true even when both operands have the same bit pattern.
Do not special-case only zero: the guard must reject all floating-point types before try_to_scalar_int.
Eq and Ne map to different boolean values (TRUE vs FALSE); an incorrect proof can select the opposite branch for either.
A regression test that only checks which blocks exist can miss this; assert that the float comparison's switchInt is retained.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a MIR-opt test (here the `floats` function) with `// EMIT_MIR jump_threading.floats.JumpThreading.diff` and `// CHECK: switchInt(` so the expectation is that JumpThreading leaves the floating-point comparison's switchInt in place. Cover both panic-abort and panic-unwind MIR dumps. Use -0.0 versus 0.0 to exercise bit-pattern/equality divergence, and add NaN and Ne variants for stronger coverage. The expected observable result for the sample is 0 (the true branch of `x == 0.0`), not 1.
evidence: - [Fix miscompilation in the jump threading MIR optimization when comparing floats](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/128271)
// Floating point equality does not follow bit-patterns.
// -0.0 and NaN both have special rules for equality,
// and therefore we cannot use integer comparisons for them.
// Avoid handling them, though this could be extended in the future.
// Test for issue #128243, where float equality was assumed to be bitwise.
// When adding float support, it must be ensured that this continues working properly.
